questions.stem: How is Edenglassie structured?
options: Two storylines in Brisbane, one in the 1850s and one in 2024
Two storylines in Brisbane, one in 1824 and one in 1988
One storyline following a single family from 1824 to 2024
Two storylines, one in 1850s Sydney and one in present-day Brisbane
questions.explanation: The novel moves between Brisbane in the mid-1850s and Brisbane in 2024. The two stories are set nearly two centuries and about five generations apart.

questions.stem: How does the 2024 storyline begin?
options: A journalist finds Granny Eddie's name in an old colonial record
Granny Eddie trips over a tree root by the river and ends up in hospital
Winona is arrested at a protest against the city's bicentenary celebrations
Dr Johnny returns to Brisbane to look for his grandfather's family
questions.explanation: Granny Eddie Blanket, an Elder about a hundred years old, falls over a tree root near the river at South Bank. Most of her story then takes place on a hospital ward.

questions.stem: Which First Nations people does Johnny, in the present-day story, belong to?
options: The Wiradjuri
The Kaurna
The Gomeroi
The Yugambeh
questions.explanation: Johnny is a Gomeroi man, from outside Brisbane. In the 1850s story Mulanyin is Yugambeh, which is one way the novel links different peoples across time.

questions.stem: What does the journalist Dartmouth Rice want from Granny Eddie?
options: Her backing, for a protest against the bicentenary
Her memories of Tom Petrie, for a book about his life
Her help, to find a lost colonial grave site
Her life story, for Brisbane's colonial bicentenary
questions.explanation: Rice sees a big story in her as the city prepares to mark two hundred years of colonisation. Eddie spins him yarns and keeps the true story to herself.

questions.stem: Who is Mulanyin?
options: A Yagara Elder who leads his people in battle against the Native Police
A Scottish settler who learns the Yagara language as a boy
A Goorie stockman who works on a cattle station in the west
A young Yugambeh man who comes to live with the Kurilpa in Magandjin
questions.explanation: Mulanyin leaves his saltwater Country to the south and lives with his law-brother Murree's people in Magandjin, where he goes through ceremony.

questions.stem: Where does Nita work?
options: As a cook on the boats that sail up the Brisbane River
As a laundress at the old convict barracks in the town
As a teacher at a mission school north of the town
As a servant in the household of the Petrie family
questions.explanation: Nita works for the Petries, a settler family. Her place in their household shows how Aboriginal people's labour was used even by settlers who thought of themselves as kind.

questions.stem: What does Mulanyin dream of?
options: Buying a cattle station of his own beside Tom Petrie's new land
Earning enough to buy a whale boat and take Nita home to his Country
Becoming a trooper in the Native Police to protect his own family
Signing on as crew of a Sydney ship and leaving Nita behind in the town
questions.explanation: Mulanyin wants to marry Nita and return with her to his saltwater Country. The publisher says his plans for independence collide with white justice.

questions.stem: Which real event does Mulanyin witness?
options: The first landing of the convicts at Moreton Bay in 1824
The ceremony declaring Queensland a separate colony in December 1859
The opening of the first bridge across the Brisbane River
The botched public hanging of the resistance leader Dundalli
questions.explanation: Mulanyin is in the crowd at Dundalli's execution in Brisbane, and he is deeply shaken. It shows him what colonial law can do to a man who resists.

questions.stem: How are the two storylines connected, as far as reviews reveal?
options: The legacy of Nita and Mulanyin reaches into the lives of Eddie and Winona
Winona discovers that Dr Johnny is descended from the Petrie family
Granny Eddie turns out to have been born in 1854, the year Mulanyin arrives
Dartmouth Rice reveals that he is writing a history of Mulanyin's life
questions.explanation: The publisher says the legacy of Nita and Mulanyin's tragic past reaches into the modern characters' lives. Reviewers keep the full link a secret, so build arguments on place, family and echoes between the stories.

questions.stem: Who is Winona?
options: Granny Eddie's nurse, who is new to working on the hospital ward
Dr Johnny's sister, who works as a lawyer in Brisbane
A young journalist who works for Dartmouth Rice
Granny Eddie's granddaughter, a fiery activist
questions.explanation: Winona is sharp-tongued, funny and uncompromising. She wants to fight back against colonial injustice, and she clashes with almost everyone, including Johnny.

questions.stem: What is Dr Johnny's story?
options: He is tracing Mulanyin's descendants so that he can write a family history
He is reconnecting with his Gomeroi family, after his grandfather was taken as a baby
He is a Brisbane-born doctor who has grown up surrounded by his Gomeroi family
He is Winona's cousin, raised by Granny Eddie after his parents were killed in a crash
questions.explanation: Johnny's grandfather was taken from his family as a baby, so Johnny has grown up without that connection. Winona doubts whether he is Aboriginal enough, which raises questions about identity and belonging.

questions.stem: How does Granny Eddie's outlook differ from Winona's?
options: Eddie avoids speaking about the past, while Winona digs into the archives
Eddie is pragmatic and inclusive, while Winona wants to strike back hard
Eddie wants revenge on the colonists, while Winona wants to forgive them
Eddie has given up on her culture, while Winona wants to relearn it
questions.explanation: Eddie has lived a long, hard life and urges her granddaughter to avoid bitterness and bring people in. Winona's anger is just as justified, and the novel lets the two views argue.

questions.stem: How is Tom Petrie presented?
options: A missionary who forces the Goorie children to attend his church school
A convict who escaped from Moreton Bay and lived with the Goorie people
A young settler who speaks Yagara and is given land by the Elders' leave
A cruel magistrate who sentences Dundalli and the other resistance fighters
questions.explanation: Tom Petrie learned Yagara and Goorie customs and was allowed to select land for a cattle station. Lucashenko uses him to imagine how colonists might have worked with Aboriginal people rather than against them.

questions.stem: Mrs Petrie criticises slavery in the United States. Why is this ironic?
options: She has just returned from America, where she supported slavery
She has freed the Aboriginal servants who once worked in her house
She lives on taken land with Aboriginal people working in her house
She was transported to Moreton Bay as a convict and forced to labour
questions.explanation: Mrs Petrie condemns injustice far away while benefiting from it at home. Her moral confidence blinds her to the dispossession around her.

questions.stem: What does the title Edenglassie refer to?
options: An early colonial name for part of Brisbane, blending Edinburgh and Glasgow
A Yagara word for the river that runs through the centre of Brisbane
The name of the Petrie family's new farm on the land the Elders gave them
The ship that carried the first convicts from England to Moreton Bay
questions.explanation: Edenglassie joins the names of two Scottish cities, and it was used briefly for part of Brisbane. Readers may also hear Eden in it, a lost paradise.

questions.stem: Why is the 1850s an important moment for the historical storyline?
options: Convicts still outnumber free settlers, and transportation is at its height
Queensland has become a separate colony with its own parliament and army
The Native Police have just been disbanded, and frontier violence is easing
Aboriginal people still outnumber the colonists, and the future is unsettled
questions.explanation: Convict transportation to Moreton Bay had ended, but Queensland was not yet a separate colony. Goorie people still outnumbered the newcomers and hoped they might leave, which makes the period feel open.

questions.stem: Dundalli, whose execution the novel depicts, was:
options: a Yugambeh Elder who signed a treaty with the colonists in 1840
a Native Police trooper who deserted to join the Goorie resistance
a Ngugi fisherman who guided the first ships into Moreton Bay
a Dalla resistance leader hanged in public in Brisbane in 1855
questions.explanation: Dundalli was hanged on 5 January 1855. The hangman misjudged the rope and the execution was botched, before a crowd that included many Aboriginal people.

questions.stem: What was the Native Police, active in the 1850s storyline?
options: A branch of the British Army sent to keep order among the convicts
A colonial force of Aboriginal troopers under white officers, used on the frontier
A council of Aboriginal Elders who settled disputes between clans in the region
A volunteer group of settlers who protected Aboriginal camps from attack
questions.explanation: The Native Police were used against Aboriginal communities across the frontier. In the novel, its violence and settler killings press in on Mulanyin's world.

questions.stem: Which earlier novel by Melissa Lucashenko won the Miles Franklin Award?
options: Too Much Lip
Carpentaria
The Swan Book
Benang
questions.explanation: Lucashenko, a Goorie author, won the 2019 Miles Franklin Award for Too Much Lip. Edenglassie, her seventh novel, is her first historical novel.

questions.stem: Lucashenko based her Tom Petrie on a real man. What is one key source for his life?
options: His evidence at Dundalli's trial, printed in the colony's newspapers
His Reminiscences of Early Queensland, recorded by his daughter
His diary of the convict years, kept in a London archive
His letters to the Governor of New South Wales about land
questions.explanation: Tom Petrie's memories of early Brisbane were written down by his daughter Constance and published in 1904. Lucashenko drew on this record and departs from it where she chooses.

questions.stem: Why set the modern storyline in the year of Brisbane's colonial bicentenary?
options: It lets the novel celebrate how far the city has come since 1824
It shows that the city has fully recognised its First Nations history
It lets the novel honour Tom Petrie as the city's true founding father
It lets the novel ask who celebrates colonisation and whose history is told
questions.explanation: Granny Eddie is made a figurehead for the celebrations while she knows a different story. The setting sets official history against what Aboriginal families remember.

questions.stem: How do the modern characters challenge the old colonial myth of a 'dying race'?
options: They are confident, funny and politically active, and very much alive
They have lost their culture but keep their family names and land
They are shown mainly as victims, defeated by colonial history
They have assimilated, so the myth no longer applies to them
questions.explanation: Lucashenko has said her modern characters push back against the 'dying race' narrative. Eddie, Winona and Johnny show Aboriginal survival and continuity, not disappearance.

questions.stem: Granny Eddie tells the journalist that the official history is wrong. What idea does this raise?
options: Who has the right to tell history, and which sources are trusted
That journalists are the most reliable keepers of a city's past
That the past is unknowable, so no account of it can be judged
That written records should be trusted over family memory
questions.explanation: Eddie says she has the true story from the Old People. The novel sets Aboriginal knowledge passed down through families against the official, celebratory version of the past.

questions.stem: Lucashenko called Edenglassie 'a First Nations love story'. Which feature supports this?
options: Its central romance is between Granny Eddie and Dartmouth Rice
Its love is for Country alone, with no human romance in the story
It retells a famous English love story in an Australian setting
Each timeline has a romance, set against love for family and Country
questions.explanation: Mulanyin and Nita in the 1850s, and Winona and Johnny in 2024, form two romances. Around them is love for kin, community and Country.

questions.stem: What does the novel suggest about the paths history could have taken?
options: Colonisation did not have to unfold as it did, so change is possible now
Colonisation was inevitable, whatever choices individuals made at the time
Aboriginal resistance alone decided how Brisbane came to be built
The past is finished, so the present owes it nothing
questions.explanation: Lucashenko has said Tom Petrie's path did not have to go the way it did. Imagining other possibilities in the past opens the idea that things can still change.

questions.stem: Which theme does Johnny's search for his family most clearly explore?
options: Justice and the failures of colonial law and policing
Ageing, and how the city treats its oldest Elders
Identity and belonging, and who is welcomed into community
Love across class lines in colonial Brisbane society
questions.explanation: Johnny's ties to his family were broken by the taking of his grandfather. Winona doubts him, while Eddie argues for bringing people home.

questions.stem: What is the effect of moving between the two timelines?
options: The past and present comment on each other, showing history's legacy
The modern story shows that colonial harm has been healed and left behind
The modern story is shown to be a dream of a character in the past
The historical story is shown to be a novel that Winona is writing
questions.explanation: Placing 1855 beside 2024 shows how dispossession still shapes lives, and how culture and resistance have continued. Each story deepens the other.

questions.stem: How does the tone of the two storylines differ?
options: Both storylines are satirical, mocking the colonists throughout
The modern story is often comic, while the historical one is more realist
The modern story is bleak, while the historical one is light and romantic
Both storylines are comic, with colonial violence kept offstage
questions.explanation: Lucashenko uses humour to make her modern characters fully rounded, and to push back against stereotypes. The 1850s chapters show colonial violence more directly.

questions.stem: The novel uses words such as dagai for white people and calls the Brisbane River the Warrar. What is the effect?
options: It marks the words as foreign, so the Goorie characters seem exotic
It suggests the languages were lost after the 1850s storyline
It centres a Goorie point of view and shows that the languages endure
It shows that the characters cannot speak or understand English
questions.explanation: Using Aboriginal words places the reader inside a Goorie view of the world. Colonists become the outsiders, and the land keeps its older names.

questions.stem: Spirits and ancestors play a part in the novel. How might a reader best understand this?
options: As a sign that Granny Eddie is confused after her fall by the river
As part of a Goorie worldview in which ancestors and Country stay present
As Gothic horror elements, meant to frighten the reader
As symbols of the guilt that haunts the settler characters
questions.explanation: Ancestors and spirits are woven through the story. Reading them as part of a living worldview fits the novel better than treating them as fantasy.

questions.stem: At the end of the novel, Lucashenko adds an author's note. What does it do?
options: It retells the main events from Granny Eddie's point of view
It separates the real people and events from those she invented
It explains that the Petries are characters she invented
It reveals that the whole story was told to her by Tom Petrie's family
questions.explanation: The note shows which people and events are drawn from history, such as Dundalli and the Petries. It reminds readers that the novel is fiction built on real events.

questions.stem: Who says 'Marry me, Nita. Come away from this place', and what does it show?
options: Tom Petrie, asking Nita to stay on at his new cattle station
Dr Johnny, joking with Winona about an old family story
Dundalli, speaking to the crowd just before his execution
Mulanyin, dreaming of taking Nita home to his own Country
questions.explanation: Mulanyin's proposal shows his love for Nita and his wish to take her away from the Petrie household and colonial Brisbane, back to his saltwater Country.

questions.stem: Granny Eddie says, 'We bring people in, we bring our Mob home'. What does it show?
options: Her refusal to let anyone outside the family hear her stories
Her belief in welcoming back people cut off from their families
Her view that the Mob should be limited to those raised in culture
Her wish to share the family's true story with the journalist
questions.explanation: Eddie says this when Winona rejects Johnny. It shows an inclusive idea of community that makes room for people whose family ties were broken.

questions.stem: Granny Eddie is promoted as 'Queensland's Oldest Aboriginal'. What is the effect of the phrase?
options: It is a proud title that Eddie chose for herself many years ago
It is sincere praise, showing the city honouring its Elders
It is a nickname that Winona gives her to tease her
It is ironic: the media turns a living Elder into a curiosity
questions.explanation: The label treats Eddie as a record-breaker and a symbol for the celebrations. It ignores her as a person and the history she carries, which the novel exposes with humour.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Edenglassie shows that the past is never really past.' Discuss.
options: Lucashenko shows that the dispossession of the 1850s still shapes the lives of Eddie and Winona
Edenglassie is a novel by Melissa Lucashenko that has two storylines set in Brisbane
This essay will discuss the past and present in Edenglassie by Melissa Lucashenko
In Edenglassie, Granny Eddie falls over a tree root near the river at South Bank and goes to hospital
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Mulanyin watches Dundalli being hanged.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Add the exact date of the hanging and the name of the hangman who did it
List the other people who were in the crowd on the day
Retell what Mulanyin does in the chapters after the hanging
Explain how the execution shows Mulanyin what colonial law does to those who resist
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Linking the hanging to the threat colonial law poses to Mulanyin connects the event to the novel's ideas about power and resistance.
